newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britain agonises over gun law after Dunblane.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britain agonises over gun law after Dunblane.

text.p: Just days after a lone gunman shot dead 35 people in Tasmania in April, a stunned Australian government vowed to bring in tough new gun laws.
But in phlegmatic Britain, government reaction was more measured.

After a loner called Thomas Hamilton, armed with four handguns, walked into a school in the Scottish town of Dunblane and killed 16 children and their teacher, calls for immediate curbs on firearms were brushed aside as emotional extravagance.
Instead, a senior judge was appointed to investigate the March massacre and private ownership of guns.

Lord Cullen is to present his report to the government on October 14 after what has been described as the "Herculean task" of weighing up submissions from dozens of people, including parents of the Dunblane victims and the highly vocal gun lobby.
His conclusions have only been guessed at. One tabloid newspaper declared that Cullen will recommend a ban on handguns, but others predict he will tread a softer line.
Whatever his recommendations, there is little doubting the strength of support for a ban on handguns in Britain. Opinion polls show 70 percent in favour.

A parliamentary committee appointed to look into the merits of outlawing handguns emerged from its deliberations in August split between the six Conservative members of parliament who opposed any ban -- and passed a report rejecting one -- and five from the opposition Labour Party who favoured outlawing guns.
There was outrage from the press and public. Conservatives were accused of caving in to the gun lobby and of callous disregard for the feelings of those affected by Dunblane.
"I'm very upset at being characterised as some sort of mass murderer by some tabloid newspapers," said a shaken Walter Sweeney, one of the Conservative MP's who opposed a ban.
The six Conservatives appeared to have gravely underestimated the depth of feeling in a country that went into shock after Hamilton's calculated crime.

On the day that MPs announced their conclusions, an anti-gun group took out full-page newspaper advertisements showing a photograph of Emma Crozier, one of the 16 five- and six-year old victims of the Dunblane massacre.

Above her young, smiling face were the words: "No more picnics, no more days on the beach, no more butterflies, no more choccie cake, no more bedtime stories, no more teddy bears, no more kisses good night...No More Guns."

About 800,000 firearms certificates, which must be renewed annually, are issued every year. Britons found in possession of illegal firearms can face sentences of up to 10 years in prison and heavy fines.

Certificates are issued by the police. People applying for a licence must satisfy authorities they have a good reason to keep a firearm, that they can be trusted and that public safety will not be threatened. Applicants must keep the weapons in a safe.

Most Britons believe regulations are still not strict enough. Aware of the vote-winning potential of the issue, the opposition Labour Party has pledged to make handguns illegal if it wins the general election, due by next May.

Right-wing Conservatives, who are widely believed to identify with the gun lobby because hunting and shooting are largely sports of the upper classes, say a ban would be an infringement of liberties and would be ineffective anyway.
According to Peter Squires, lecturer in social policy and criminal justice at the University of Brighton in southeast England, Cullen is likely to stop short of advocating a ban on handguns.

Squires believes Cullen will instead recommend that privately-owned weapons are stored at gun clubs -- while their owners keep ammunition and firing mechanisms separately -- and propose much tougher procedures for getting a licence.

Hamilton held licences for the semi-automatic pistols he used in the Dunblane massacre, even though he was regarded as an unstable character and had been reported to the police several times because of his strange behaviour with young boys.
Nine years earlier, Michael Ryan had shot dead 16 people, including his own mother, in the southern English town of Hungerford. He too held licences for his guns.
Both men shot themselves at the scenes of their crimes.
All Ryan and Hamilton had to do to get their licences was to fill out a form, get one signature from a gun club member and then pass it on to police for checks.
A 1988 law prohibits people who have been jailed for more than three years from having a certificate.
Crimes involving the use of handguns rose by 142 percent in Britain in the decade to 1994, but Squires argues that outlawing firarms would do little to reduce gun crime.
"The evidence is that making guns illegal merely increases recourse to illegal guns," he said.

The vast majority of crimes involving firearms are carried out with illegal weapons, of which there are thought to be three or four times more in Britain than legal ones. A study carried out by London police found that of 55 firearms recovered from crime scenes, only two had ever been licensed, he said.
Australia's experience shows that even if Britain chooses to outlaw guns, the process will not be easy.
After a long battle, Prime Minister John Howard had to threaten a national referendum on his proposed new gun laws to force three state governments to step into line.

Under pressure from hunters and farmers, the states wanted to allow gun-owners to keep modified pump action and semi-automatic shotguns which could fire only two shells at a time. But with polls showing 90 percent of Australians in favour of new gun laws, they stood little chance of winning a referendum.
Australian gun owners are now threatening to simply hide their guns.
